# Motor drug therapy
Source: https://llmsx.org/tree/parkinson-s-disease-motor-drug-therapy-levodopa-dopamine-agonists-mao-b-comt-a2a-drugs-fluctuations-dyskinesia-gait-and-medication-safety/

> Motor drug therapy: levodopa, dopamine agonists, MAO-B/COMT/A2A drugs, fluctuations, dyskinesia, gait and medication safety. 8 concept packs; the section's 131 claims are in llms-facts.txt#parkinson-s-disease-motor-drug-therapy-levodopa-dopamine-agonists-mao-b-comt-a2a-drugs-fluctuations-dyskinesia-gait-and-medication-safety.

## Amantadine, anticholinergics and other adjunct drugs

Amantadine has formulation-specific evidence for dyskinesia, while its precise therapeutic mechanism remains unknown. Extended-release Gocovri requires attention to renal function, hallucinations, edema and withdrawal. Anticholinergics such as benztropine and trihexyphenidyl have a restricted role because cognitive and peripheral adverse effects can outweigh motor benefit, especially in older people. Clinical emphasis on tremor should be distinguished from the weak trial evidence for preferential tremor efficacy. Older inconclusive amantadine reviews address different evidence from later formulation-specific trials. NICE discourages several proposed neuroprotective supplements.

- [statement] The 2003 Cochrane amantadine review found insufficient evidence for efficacy and safety for general idiopathic Parkinson symptoms from older trials; its searches extended through 2001, so that conclusion does not include the 2017 EASE LID dyskinesia trial. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8715353/
- [statement] In the 2017 EASE LID trial, the week 12 placebo-adjusted improvement in Unified Dyskinesia Rating Scale score was 7.9 points. This is evidence for the studied extended-release product and population, rather than proof that every amantadine formulation is equivalent. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5710325/
- [statement] Benztropine and trihexyphenidyl are anticholinergic options used particularly in younger patients; cognitive impairment, confusion, hallucinations, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation and urinary retention restrict their usefulness, especially with advancing age. (medium confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/treatment/prescription-medications/anticholinergic-drugs
- [statement] Hallucinations, peripheral edema and dizziness were prominent adverse events in EASE LID; Gocovri prescribing information also lists these adverse reactions. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5710325/
- [statement] The Parkinson Foundation describes anticholinergics as predominantly useful for tremor with little effect on other symptoms; the Cochrane review found motor benefit over placebo but conflicting results and insufficient support for a preferential effect on tremor. The latter limits claims of established symptom selectivity. (medium confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/treatment/prescription-medications/anticholinergic-drugs

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/amantadine-anticholinergics-and-other-adjunct-drugs/ · 13 claims from 5 sources

## Dopamine agonists and apomorphine

Dopamine agonists offer symptomatic treatment for selected patients with Parkinson disease. Early-treatment choices require balancing motor benefit against sleepiness, hallucinations, and orthostatic hypotension; formulation choice should reflect patient preferences and tolerability. Apomorphine has distinct intermittent subcutaneous rescue and continuous infusion uses in advanced disease. The TOLEDO randomized trial supports infusion for persistent motor fluctuations, but adverse effects and treatment withdrawal remain relevant. Product-specific supervision, contraindications, and infusion-site care are essential. The PROUD trial did not support disease modification by pramipexole.

- [statement] In the PROUD delayed-start trial, clinical and neuroimaging outcomes did not support a disease-modifying effect of pramipexole, consistent with the AAN guideline assessment of dopamine agonist trials. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23726851/
- [statement] Both US apomorphine labels contraindicate concomitant use with ondansetron, listed among serotonin receptor antagonists, because profound hypotension and loss of consciousness have been reported. (medium confidence) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2026/214056s005.pdf
- [statement] Dopamine agonists require monitoring for daytime somnolence, sudden sleep onset, hallucinations, nausea, and orthostatic hypotension; these are also explicit apomorphine-label safety concerns. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8672433/
- [statement] The AAN found no strong evidence favoring ropinirole over pramipexole or extended-release over immediate-release pramipexole for early-PD motor efficacy; formulation, administration route, cost, and patient preferences should guide selection. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8672433/
- [statement] ONAPGO prescribing information revised May 2026 describes subcutaneous infusion for motor fluctuations in adults with advanced PD; it explicitly states that ONAPGO is not substitutable for apomorphine products intended for intermittent use. (low confidence) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2026/214056s005.pdf

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/dopamine-agonists-and-apomorphine/ · 11 claims from 5 sources

## Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation

Impulse control disorders in Parkinson’s disease include harmful gambling, shopping, sexual behaviour and binge eating. Dopamine dysregulation syndrome involves compulsive medication overuse; punding involves repetitive, purposeless activity. Dopamine agonists carry a major ICD risk, although other dopaminergic therapy can also be implicated. Prevention requires candid patient and family counselling and repeated behavioural review. Management generally starts with specialist-guided gradual agonist reduction, while watching motor control and withdrawal. DDS can require a different medication-reduction strategy. Specialist cognitive behavioural therapy may help persistent ICDs, but trial limitations and endpoint-dependent drug results argue against overstating treatment certainty.

- [statement] NICE recommends specialist cognitive behavioural therapy directed at ICDs when changing dopaminergic treatment is ineffective. A small randomized waiting-list-controlled trial supports short-term improvement in patient symptom severity. (medium confidence) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations
- [statement] Dopamine dysregulation syndrome (DDS) involves compulsive use of dopamine replacement medication beyond motor requirements, with drug seeking or hoarding, social impairment and sometimes mood elevation; distress can emerge when doses are reduced. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1736875/
- [statement] Punding is a related repetitive, non-goal-directed behaviour, such as repeatedly sorting, assembling or disassembling objects; it and DDS are related to, but distinguishable from, the usual gambling, shopping, eating and sexual ICDs. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11098885/
- [statement] Dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome can complicate tapering, with anxiety, panic, depression or dysphoria, fatigue and pain; symptoms may be refractory to levodopa replacement. Its recognition matters because it can prevent successful agonist withdrawal. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5077247/
- [statement] In Parkinson’s disease, clinically important impulse control disorders include compulsive gambling, shopping, sexual behaviour and binge eating; these behaviours can cause serious financial and psychosocial harm. (medium confidence) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/impulse-control-disorders-and-dopamine-dysregulation/ · 15 claims from 6 sources

## Levodopa and carbidopa formulations and delivery

Levodopa supplies the dopamine precursor, while carbidopa reduces peripheral conversion and associated nausea. Delivery options include immediate- and controlled-release tablets, extended-release capsules, intestinal carbidopa-levodopa infusion, subcutaneous foscarbidopa/foslevodopa infusion, and intermittent inhaled levodopa. Extended-release oral formulations aim to sustain benefit with fewer dosing occasions, but conversion requires formulation-specific titration. Infusions can provide sustained delivery while adding tube, pump, procedure, or skin-site burdens. Inhaled levodopa addresses OFF episodes alongside existing carbidopa/levodopa treatment. RISE-PD supports IPX203 over immediate-release treatment in patients with fluctuations; it does not establish prevention of future motor complications. Product-specific labels distinguish routes, dose equivalence, and delivery limitations. Regulatory status of subcutaneous ND0612 is time-sensitive: a US complete response letter was announced on October 23, 2025, and EU marketing authorization was announced in April 2026.

- [statement] Levodopa is converted to dopamine in the brain. Carbidopa inhibits peripheral levodopa decarboxylation, increasing levodopa availability to the brain and reducing peripheral nausea and vomiting; it does not remove central levodopa adverse effects. (high confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/treatment/prescription-medications/levodopa
- [statement] Foscarbidopa and foslevodopa are prodrugs converted in vivo to carbidopa and levodopa. The October 2024 VYALEV label indicates subcutaneous pump infusion for motor fluctuations in adults with advanced Parkinson’s disease. (high confidence) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2024/216962s000lbl.pdf
- [statement] Conversion from immediate-release carbidopa-levodopa to CREXONT is not a 1:1 dose substitution; use formulation-specific conversion and titration rather than matching milligrams. (high confidence) — https://crexont.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/CREXONT-Full-Prescribing-Information-August-2024.pdf
- [statement] Inhaled levodopa (INBRIJA) is an intermittent treatment for OFF episodes in patients already treated with carbidopa/levodopa, rather than a stand-alone maintenance formulation. (high confidence) — https://www.inbrija.com/prescribing-information.pdf
- [statement] CREXONT contains immediate-release carbidopa/levodopa granules and extended-release levodopa pellets, combining rapid and sustained delivery within an oral capsule. (high confidence) — https://crexont.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/CREXONT-Full-Prescribing-Information-August-2024.pdf

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/levodopa-and-carbidopa-formulations-and-delivery/ · 23 claims from 12 sources

## MAO-B, COMT inhibitors and adenosine A2A antagonists

MAO-B inhibitors preserve dopamine activity; COMT inhibitors prolong levodopa availability; istradefylline targets adenosine A2A receptors. These classes offer distinct adjunct approaches to OFF episodes, with modest and drug-dependent benefits. Selegiline and rasagiline also have early-disease symptomatic evidence, but rasagiline disease modification is unconfirmed. Safinamide and opicapone have supportive adjunct trials, while istradefylline evidence assessments differ between the MDS review and EMA’s refusal assessment. Selection requires attention to dosing burden, hepatic function, interactions and dyskinesia. Tolcapone carries a serious liver-injury concern. Receptor selectivity does not remove psychiatric or dyskinesia risks. The claims distinguish symptom improvement from disease modification and diary-time benefit from quality-of-life improvement.

- [statement] Rasagiline reduces OFF time as an adjunct; the MDS review describes placebo-adjusted reductions of 0.5–0.9 hours/day and rates it likely efficacious, while noting that the average OFF-time improvement did not meet its clinical-meaningfulness threshold. (medium confidence) — https://movementdisorders.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mds.30162
- [statement] Safinamide adjunct trials support reduced OFF time and increased ON time without troublesome dyskinesia; the MDS review describes benefits around one hour compared with placebo, although individual trials vary. (medium confidence) — https://movementdisorders.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mds.30162
- [statement] Safinamide inhibits MAO-B and thereby reduces dopamine catabolism; additional effects on glutamate release and sodium channels have been described, but their added clinical relevance remains uncertain. (medium confidence) — https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/fda/fdaDrugXsl.cfm?setid=c4d65f28-983f-42b4-bb23-023ae0fe81b2
- [statement] ADAGIO found a possible disease-modifying signal at 1 mg/day but not 2 mg/day and urged caution, while the clinical review reports that long-term follow-up did not confirm disease modification. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19776408/
- [statement] Safinamide and opicapone can cause or worsen dyskinesia when added to levodopa; both US labels state that reducing levodopa or another dopaminergic drug may mitigate it. (medium confidence) — https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/fda/fdaDrugXsl.cfm?setid=c4d65f28-983f-42b4-bb23-023ae0fe81b2

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/mao-b-comt-inhibitors-and-adenosine-a2a-antagonists/ · 20 claims from 6 sources

## Motor fluctuations, wearing-off and dyskinesia management

Motor fluctuations divide the day into periods of useful medication benefit (ON) and returning symptoms (OFF). Wearing-off, delayed ON, sudden OFF and dose failure represent different patterns; peak-dose and diphasic dyskinesia also differ in their timing. Management requires specialist assessment and balancing symptom control against involuntary movements. Common approaches include adjusting dose intervals, reducing individual doses when appropriate, and escalating treatment when control remains inadequate. Coexisting dyskinesia and OFF may require fractionation rather than simply reducing medication. Patient goals, tolerability, disability and quality of life matter alongside time-based outcomes. The 2025 MDS evidence categories describe strength of evidence and should not be interpreted as a treatment sequence.

- [statement] For fluctuations inadequately controlled by oral medication, infusion therapies can be considered; the MDS review supports selected continuous-delivery treatments as likely efficacious, rather than guaranteeing benefit for every patient. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7851275/
- [statement] A common initial strategy for wearing-off is to shorten the interval between levodopa doses. Practical schedule adjustments are widely used, but the 2025 MDS review notes that not all have been tested in randomized trials. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7851275/
- [statement] If schedule adjustments do not sufficiently improve motor fluctuations, additional medical treatment may be needed; persistent inadequate control can prompt consideration of pump therapy or a neurosurgical procedure. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7851275/
- [statement] NICE advises against deep brain stimulation when best medical therapy adequately controls symptoms, and recommends considering it when advanced disease is not adequately controlled; the MDS review also describes escalation when less invasive options provide insufficient benefit. (medium confidence) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations
- [statement] NICE advises considering amantadine when dyskinesia is not adequately managed by modifying existing therapy; the Aradi–Hauser review likewise includes it among options for peak-dose dyskinesia. (medium confidence) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/motor-fluctuations-wearing-off-and-dyskinesia-management/ · 17 claims from 4 sources

## PD medication timing, interactions and hospital safety

Medication safety in Parkinson disease depends on preserving individualized dose times, avoiding abrupt interruption, planning administration during fasting or swallowing problems, and checking medicines that block dopamine or interact with the existing regimen. NICE and hospital safety resources emphasize appropriate timing, specialist involvement and accurate medication records. Pharmacy recommendations address reconciliation, custom order times, alerts, medicine availability and careful substitution. Protein redistribution requires nutritional safeguards. Antiemetic choice must account for drug-specific contraindications. Observational evidence about whether medication delays prolong hospital stay is conflicting, so hospital length-of-stay findings should not be presented as universal causal effects.

- [statement] Observational findings on medication delays and hospital length of stay conflict: Martinez-Ramirez and colleagues reported longer stays with delayed or missed doses, whereas Skelly and colleagues found no adjusted association; these findings do not establish that delays invariably prolong admission. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4401689/
- [statement] A pharmacy-informatics review states that medications affecting dopaminergic states must be used cautiously in Parkinson's disease, and singles out dopamine antagonists in the antipsychotic class (including haloperidol) and the antiemetic class (including metoclopramide, promethazine and prochlorperazine) as able to worsen Parkinson motor function. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10682362/
- [statement] NICE NG71 states that people with Parkinson's disease who are admitted to hospital or care homes should have their medicines given at the appropriate times, which in some cases may mean allowing self-medication, and adjusted by, or only after discussion with, a specialist in the management of Parkinson's disease; a pharmacy-informatics review describes electronic order entry that can mistranscribe a patient's specific medication times and intervals. (medium confidence) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations
- [statement] A pharmacy-informatics review proposes that, when adding a medicine to the hospital formulary is not feasible, the inpatient pharmacy identify patient-owned supplies and have them re-labeled for use during the stay, and it notes that the FDA Orange Book defines therapeutic equivalency; the Parkinson's Foundation safe and contraindicated medications document states that medications, even in the same class, are usually not interchangeable and that patients should be allowed to supply their own medications if not on formulary. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10682362/
- [statement] The Foundation cautions that benzodiazepines and other medicines for sleep or pain can contribute to confusion, hallucinations and falls; its acute-agitation advice limits repeated benzodiazepine use to avoid worsening confusion. (low confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/sites/default/files/documents/safe-contraindicated-medications-2026.pdf

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/pd-medication-timing-interactions-and-hospital-safety/ · 15 claims from 6 sources

## Tremor, gait, freezing and postural instability management

Tremor and axial disability require symptom-specific assessment. Levodopa is the principal drug approach for troublesome tremor, and apparent resistance can reflect inadequate treatment delivery. Persistent disabling tremor can warrant specialist invasive-treatment assessment. Freezing must be assessed in relation to medication state: OFF, pseudo-ON and true ON freezing need different interpretations. Reducing OFF time may help OFF freezing, but persistent gait and balance problems also require Parkinson-specific physiotherapy. Rivastigmine gait findings are promising phase 2 evidence rather than established freezing treatment. Methylphenidate evidence is inconsistent, with a negative randomized trial despite permissive consensus guidance.

- [statement] For residual tremor, anticholinergics have only a restricted role in young cognitively intact patients, propranolol has limited supporting evidence, and clozapine may help but requires specialist safety monitoring because of serious adverse effects. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10041452/
- [statement] Freezing treatment studies are difficult to compare when they omit subtype classification or rely on a single rating-scale item; identifying the freezing phenotype and measuring freezing directly are important to interpretation. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11561004/
- [statement] In the Espay randomized crossover trial, methylphenidate did not improve gait and tended to worsen motor function, sleepiness and quality of life; this negative trial limits extrapolation from positive open-label observations. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3068005/
- [statement] Disabling tremor that persists despite optimized medication can justify specialist assessment for invasive treatment, including deep brain stimulation; the tremor review also identifies focused ultrasound as an option. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10041452/
- [statement] The German consensus guideline allows methylphenidate to be considered for freezing, whereas the Espay trial authors report no gait benefit and a tendency toward worse outcomes; this is a difference between a permissive recommendation and a negative trial in a specific population. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11561004/

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/tremor-gait-freezing-and-postural-instability-management/ · 12 claims from 5 sources

# Disease-modification research

## Alpha-synuclein aggregation inhibitors and buntanetap

Covers three alpha-synuclein-directed small molecules: buntanetap (a translation inhibitor), minzasolmin (a misfolding inhibitor) and anle138b (an oligomer modulator). Buntanetap's Phase 3 early-PD study did not meet its primary endpoint per the paper and Alzforum; its cognition findings are post hoc. UCB announced that ORCHESTRA did not meet primary or secondary endpoints and began ending the minzasolmin extension. Anle138b has reported phase 1 safety data, with efficacy trials described as planned.

- [statement] Alzforum states the company did not report on the primary endpoint in the group as a whole when it announced results on July 2, 2024; Fierce Biotech says the release skirted the question of whether buntanetap moved the needle on the main goal. (high confidence) — https://www.alzforum.org/therapeutics/buntanetap
- [statement] Buntanetap, formerly Posiphen, is described as a small molecule that inhibits translation of aggregation-prone proteins including APP, tau and α-synuclein; Alzforum notes Posiphen reportedly blocks translation of α-synuclein mRNA. (high confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s44400-026-00148-x
- [statement] ORCHESTRA (NCT04658186) was a Phase 2a, randomised, placebo-controlled, 18-month study of oral minzasolmin at 180mg/day or 360mg/day versus placebo in early-stage Parkinson’s disease, with primary endpoint progression in the MDS-UPDRS Parts I–III sum score. (high confidence) — https://www.ucb.com/newsroom/press-releases/article/findings-from-minzasolmin-proof-of-concept-orchestra-study-shape-next-steps-in-ucb-parkinson-s-research-program
- [statement] UCB announced on 16 December 2024 that ORCHESTRA, a study of minzasolmin, an oral small-molecule alpha-synuclein misfolding inhibitor, did not meet its primary and secondary clinical endpoints in early Parkinson’s disease. (high confidence) — https://www.ucb.com/newsroom/press-releases/article/findings-from-minzasolmin-proof-of-concept-orchestra-study-shape-next-steps-in-ucb-parkinson-s-research-program
- [statement] UCB states it has initiated measures to terminate the extension phase of the minzasolmin program, and Alzforum and the Michael J. Fox Foundation state that the companies terminated the long-term extension or do not plan to continue testing. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.ucb.com/newsroom/press-releases/article/findings-from-minzasolmin-proof-of-concept-orchestra-study-shape-next-steps-in-ucb-parkinson-s-research-program

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/alpha-synuclein-aggregation-inhibitors-and-buntanetap/ · 16 claims from 9 sources

## Anti-alpha-synuclein immunotherapy: prasinezumab and vaccines

Prasinezumab binds aggregated alpha-synuclein; its PADOVA trial in early-stage Parkinson's disease did not meet the primary endpoint, and a Phase 3 trial is registered as recruiting. Cinpanemab's SPARK trial was stopped for lack of efficacy. AC Immune's active vaccine ACI-7104.056 is in Phase 2, with sponsor-reported interim biomarker trends.

- [statement] A Nature Medicine analysis compared the PASADENA open-label extension with an external comparator cohort from the PPMI observational study; the authors describe it as an exploratory analysis that requires confirmation in future studies. (high confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-024-03270-6
- [statement] In PADOVA, the primary endpoint of time to confirmed motor progression was not met: Roche reports HR=0.84 and p=0.0657, and the Lancet paper reports a non-significant delay in motor progression with prasinezumab versus placebo. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-05-30) — https://www.roche.com/media/releases/med-cor-2024-12-19
- [statement] Roche announced its decision to proceed with Phase III development of prasinezumab, and a Michael J. Fox Foundation news page described the drug as moving into the Phase III stage of clinical trials. (high confidence) (verified as of 2025-06-17) — https://www.roche.com/media/releases/med-cor-2025-06-16
- [statement] PADOVA is a Phase 2b, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study in which individuals with early-stage PD on stable symptomatic monotherapy (levodopa or MAO-Bi) receive intravenous prasinezumab 1500 mg every 4 weeks. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39798255/
- [statement] The registry record lists NCT07174310 (PARAISO) with phase PHASE3, overall status RECRUITING, an ACTUAL start date of 2025-11-24 and an ESTIMATED primary completion date of 2029-06-30. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT07174310

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/anti-alpha-synuclein-immunotherapy-prasinezumab-and-vaccines/ · 16 claims from 11 sources

## Disease-modification trial landscape and lessons from failed trials

Recent reviews state that no disease-modifying therapy for Parkinson's disease has been established. This concept collects registry and journal results from trials that did not show disease modification (SURE-PD3 inosine, STEADY-PD III isradipine, FAIRPARK-II deferiprone, SPARK cinpanemab) and, separately, the reasons reviewers give for such failures: symptomatic effects confound disease-modification readouts, delayed-start interpretation is contested, target engagement rarely coincided with clinical benefit in one review, and authors cite patient variability, late-stage pathology and insensitive endpoints. It also notes a post hoc re-analysis that disputes a clean negative reading of isradipine and a proposed multi-arm, multi-stage platform trial.

- [statement] Reviewers report that disease-modification trials in neurodegenerative disorders have struggled to separate symptomatic effects of putative agents from disease modification, and that documenting a disease-modifying effect is difficult for a Parkinson's disease drug with symptomatic benefit. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4910262/
- [statement] Recent reviews state that no disease-modifying therapy for Parkinson's disease has been established: one says there are currently no disease-modifying therapies (DMTs), and a trial-pipeline analysis says there are still no treatments to modify the course of the disease. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-07-17) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-026-01483-9
- [statement] SURE-PD3 (NCT02642393), a phase 3 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of inosine in early Parkinson's disease, randomized 298 participants and closed early after a prespecified interim futility analysis; the authors report MDS-UPDRS progression of 11.1 points per year with inosine versus 9.9 with placebo (P = .18). (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34519802/
- [statement] STEADY-PD III (NCT02168842), a phase 3 trial that randomized 336 patients with early Parkinson's disease to isradipine 5 mg twice daily or placebo for 36 months, reported adjusted least-squares mean changes in total UPDRS of 2.99 versus 3.26 points (treatment effect —0.27; P = 0.85), and its authors conclude that isradipine did not slow clinical progression. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7465126/
- [statement] In FAIRPARK-II (NCT02655315), a phase 2 trial in participants with newly diagnosed Parkinson's disease who had never received levodopa, the authors report that the mean MDS-UPDRS total score worsened by 15.6 points with deferiprone and 6.3 points with placebo (difference, 9.3 points; 95% confidence interval, 6.3 to 12.2; P<0.001) at 36 weeks, and the trial team's statement likewise reports greater deterioration with deferiprone than with placebo. (high confidence) — https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2209254

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/disease-modification-trial-landscape-and-lessons-from-failed-trials/ · 16 claims from 12 sources

## GBA1, ambroxol and lysosomal-targeted therapies

GBA1 variants are among the most common genetic risk factors for Parkinson's disease, so drugs aimed at the GCase lysosomal pathway have been tested as possible disease-modifying treatments. An open-label phase 2 ambroxol trial reported CSF penetration. Three later randomised trials reported no benefit on their primary outcomes: venglustat (MOVES-PD), ambroxol in Parkinson disease dementia, and Bial's BIA 28-6156 (ACTIVATE), which Bial then discontinued. The phase 3 ambroxol trial ASPro-PD was initiated in 2025. The registry lists the CAP-003 gene therapy trial as withdrawn. This is a research summary, not clinical advice.

- [statement] MOVES-PD, which evaluated the glucosylceramide synthase inhibitor venglustat, was described as unsuccessful in a Movement Disorders review, and its authors report that venglustat showed no beneficial treatment effect compared with placebo. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13518287/
- [statement] In a 52-week phase 2 randomised trial of ambroxol in Parkinson disease dementia, 55 patients were randomised and the authors report no evidence to suggest differences between groups on primary or secondary outcomes. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2025-08-01) — https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/2835760
- [statement] Bial's ACTIVATE phase 2 study was announced as testing two fixed-dose levels of BIA 28-6156 (10mg and 60mg/day), an allosteric activator of GCase, against placebo, with clinical progression assessed for up to 78 weeks of double-blind treatment. (medium confidence) — https://www.biospace.com/bial-r-and-amp-d-announces-first-patient-dosed-in-its-phase-2-clinical-trial-of-bia-28-6156-to-treat-parkinson-s-disease-patients-with-a-pathogenic-variant-in-the-glucocerebrosidase-gba1-gene
- [statement] Secondary reports on the Parkinson disease dementia ambroxol trial note that the sample size for GBA1 variant carriers was too small to say for certain that apparent improvements were real, and they list recruiting more GBA1 carriers for future studies. (medium confidence) — https://lbda.org/trial-results-ambroxol-safe-in-pdd-but-no-clear-evidence-of-benefit
- [statement] The ASPro-PD protocol describes a phase 3, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of high-dose ambroxol that will enrol 330 PD patients with confirmed GBA1 status. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12916515/

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/gba1-ambroxol-and-lysosomal-targeted-therapies/ · 16 claims from 9 sources

## GLP-1 agonists and drug repurposing in PD

GLP-1 receptor agonists, developed for diabetes, were tested in Parkinson's disease after preclinical neuroprotection findings and small trials. A single-centre exenatide phase II trial and a phase 2 lixisenatide trial reported motor benefits. The larger exenatide phase 3 trial reported no evidence of disease modification at 96 weeks. The Lancet later issued an Expression of Concern on that paper after a regulatory inspection at a trial site, with an investigation pending. Open issues are phase 2 to phase 3 translation, target engagement and subgroup selection.

- [statement] The authors of the phase 2 lixisenatide trial report that at 12 months MDS-UPDRS part III scores had changed by -0.04 points with lixisenatide and 3.04 points with placebo (difference, 3.08; 95% confidence interval, 0.86 to 5.30; P = 0.007). (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38598572/
- [statement] The authors of the phase 3 exenatide trial state that they found no evidence to support exenatide as a disease-modifying treatment for people with Parkinson's disease, and that exenatide was safe and well tolerated. (high confidence) (verified as of 2025-02-04) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39919773/
- [statement] A phase 2, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial of daily subcutaneous lixisenatide or placebo for 12 months, followed by a 2-month washout period, enrolled 156 participants diagnosed with Parkinson's disease less than 3 years earlier. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38598572/
- [statement] The stated repurposing rationale for GLP-1 receptor agonists in Parkinson's disease is neurotrophic or neuroprotective effects in preclinical models, plus epidemiological studies and small randomised trials suggesting possible benefit. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39919773/
- [statement] Exenatide-PD3 was a phase 3, multicentre, double-blind, parallel-group, randomised, placebo-controlled trial at six research hospitals in the UK that randomly assigned 194 participants to extended-release exenatide 2 mg once per week over 96 weeks or placebo. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39919773/

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/glp-1-agonists-and-drug-repurposing-in-pd/ · 14 claims from 6 sources

## LRRK2-targeted therapies: small molecule and antisense

LRRK2 (leucine-rich repeat kinase 2) is a Parkinson's disease target pursued with a small molecule inhibitor, BIIB122 (DNL151), and an intrathecal antisense oligonucleotide, BIIB094 (ION859). Biogen and Denali report that the Phase 2b LUMA study of BIIB122 in early-stage Parkinson’s disease did not meet its primary or secondary endpoints, and that they will discontinue development in idiopathic Parkinson’s disease while Denali continues the Phase 2a BEACON study in carriers of a pathogenic LRRK2 variant. The REASON phase 1 authors report cerebrospinal fluid LRRK2 and phosphorylated Rab10 lowered by up to 59% and up to 50% with BIIB094.

- [statement] Based on the LUMA results, Biogen and Denali state they will discontinue further development of BIIB122 in idiopathic Parkinson’s disease, while Denali continues the Phase 2a BEACON study in carriers of a pathogenic LRRK2 variant. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-05-21) — https://investors.biogen.com/news-releases/news-release-details/biogen-and-denali-therapeutics-provide-update-phase-2b-luma
- [statement] LUMA included individuals with early-stage Parkinson’s disease with or without a pathogenic LRRK2 variant, and MJFF describes the trial as largely including people without known genetic mutations. (high confidence) — https://investors.biogen.com/news-releases/news-release-details/biogen-and-denali-therapeutics-provide-update-phase-2b-luma
- [statement] Biogen and Denali report that the Phase 2b LUMA study of BIIB122 in early-stage Parkinson’s disease did not meet its primary or secondary endpoints. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-05-21) — https://investors.biogen.com/news-releases/news-release-details/biogen-and-denali-therapeutics-provide-update-phase-2b-luma
- [statement] A Science Translational Medicine summary states that several different LRRK2 inhibitors induced on-target histopathological changes in the lungs of nonhuman primates that were reversible after drug withdrawal and had no effect on pulmonary function; Alzforum describes three inhibitors tested at least over a period of two weeks. (high confidence) — https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/scitranslmed.aav0820
- [statement] The LUMA primary endpoint was time to confirmed worsening in the MDS-UPDRS Parts II and III combined score. (high confidence) — https://investors.biogen.com/news-releases/news-release-details/biogen-and-denali-therapeutics-provide-update-phase-2b-luma

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/lrrk2-targeted-therapies-small-molecule-and-antisense/ · 17 claims from 6 sources

## Mitochondrial and mitophagy targets: PINK1, parkin, USP30

PINK1 (a ubiquitin kinase) and parkin (an E3 ligase) flag damaged mitochondria for mitophagy, and mutations in both are linked to autosomal recessive PD. USP30, a mitochondrial deubiquitinase, opposes this pathway. Preclinical mouse and human-neuron studies support USP30 inhibition; Mission Therapeutics reports its USP30 inhibitor MTX325 has reached patients with PD in a Phase 1b study. PINK1 activators such as MTK458 are earlier-stage, and a Science Advances paper reports PINK1/Parkin-independent off-target effects for two activators.

- [statement] Parkin is an E3 ligase that functions together with the ubiquitin kinase PINK1 to flag damaged mitochondria for removal via a selective form of autophagy known as mitophagy. (high confidence) — https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.ady0240
- [statement] USP30, a deubiquitinase localized to mitochondria, antagonizes mitophagy driven by the ubiquitin ligase parkin and the protein kinase PINK1. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24896179/
- [statement] Mutations in the Parkin and PINK1 proteins are the most common form of autosomal recessive PD. (high confidence) — https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.ady0240
- [statement] Mission Therapeutics announced that the first patient has been dosed in its Phase 1b proof-of-mechanism study of MTX325, and ClinicalTrials.gov lists Part 5 (multiple doses in patients with Parkinson's Disease) as in progress. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://missiontherapeutics.com/mission-therapeutics-doses-first-parkinsons-patient-in-phase-1b-study-of-potential-disease-modifying-treatment-mtx325/
- [statement] In an αSyn-induced model, Usp30 knockout mice are reported to show protection against behavioral deficits, increased mitophagy, decreased phospho-S129 αSyn, and attenuation of SN dopaminergic neuronal loss. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10643470/

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/mitochondrial-and-mitophagy-targets-pink1-parkin-usp30/ · 14 claims from 8 sources

## Neuroinflammation: NLRP3 and microglia targets

NLRP3 inflammasome activation in microglia, which α-synuclein can drive, is a neuroinflammation target in PD. Early NLRP3 inhibitor studies of NT-0796 and selnoflast were short safety and biomarker studies, not efficacy trials. The VENT-02 registry record is TERMINATED. Minocycline and azathioprine did not meet efficacy goals, and a review says selecting participants by inflammatory phenotype could potentially enhance success.

- [statement] Dapansutrile, described as having a highly specific effect on the NLRP3 inflammasome, is in a Phase 2 trial in Parkinson's disease registered as NCT07157735 with status RECRUITING and an estimated 36 participants. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT07157735
- [statement] Exploratory analyses in the azathioprine trial suggested effects on immune biomarkers and motor symptoms, but a charity summary calls it a small proof-of-concept trial whose findings need validation in larger trials. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41389828/
- [statement] In the AZA-PD randomised, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (66 randomly assigned: azathioprine n=32, placebo n=34), the primary outcome, change in MDS-UPDRS gait-axial score in the off-state at 12 months, was not met. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41389828/
- [statement] The VENT-02 Parkinson's study registered as NCT06822517 lists incidence of treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) as its primary outcome, and its congress abstract states the primary endpoint is safety. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT06822517
- [statement] Reviews report that minocycline, which reduces microglial activation and shows therapeutic effects in PD animal models, was not progressed to phase 3 and failed to show significant therapeutic efficacy in a Phase II clinical trial. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11492043/

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/neuroinflammation-nlrp3-and-microglia-targets/ · 16 claims from 9 sources

# Rehabilitation and adjunct therapies
Source: https://llmsx.org/tree/parkinson-s-disease-rehabilitation-and-adjunct-therapies-exercise-physical-speech-and-occupational-therapy-dance-music-acupuncture-cannabis-and-supplements/

> Rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements. 8 concept packs; the section's 117 claims are in llms-facts.txt#parkinson-s-disease-rehabilitation-and-adjunct-therapies-exercise-physical-speech-and-occupational-therapy-dance-music-acupuncture-cannabis-and-supplements.

## Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD

Evidence read for acupuncture, massage, the Alexander Technique and other traditional adjuncts in Parkinson's disease (PD). Two older meta-analyses found no significant UPDRS advantage of real over placebo acupuncture; later syntheses of acupuncture combined with conventional treatment report UPDRS gains but describe the evidence as limited, and an overview rated all included reviews very-low-quality. Sham-controlled trials show a sleep signal and no fatigue benefit over sham. No serious adverse events were reported. Massage meta-analyses report motor benefit alongside methodological concerns. NICE NG71 says to consider the Alexander Technique for balance or motor function problems; a complementary-medicine guideline grades acupuncture added to drugs 'should be considered' on low-level evidence; Parkinson's UK does not endorse any particular therapies.

- [statement] NICE guideline NG71 (published 19 July 2017) recommendation 1.7.4 reads 'Consider the Alexander Technique for people with Parkinson's disease who are experiencing balance or motor function problems', and Parkinson's UK states that NICE clinical guidelines recommend that people with Parkinson's consider the Alexander technique to help with balance or motor problems (a page whose footer says 'Last updated November 2018'). (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/Recommendations
- [statement] Sham-controlled RCTs of acupuncture for PD-related fatigue found no significant difference between real and sham acupuncture: Kluger et al. (ninety-four PD patients, 6 weeks of biweekly treatment) reported significant improvements in both groups at 6 and 12 weeks without significant between-group differences, and Kong et al. (forty PD patients, 5 weeks) reported the same pattern; the Cui et al. review found fatigue showed no difference from sham (SMD 0.10) and graded certainty for fatigue very low. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27028133/
- [statement] Two systematic reviews found no significant advantage of acupuncture over placebo acupuncture on the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS): the Lee et al. review in Movement Disorders (eleven RCTs) pooled three placebo-controlled RCTs (n = 96, WMD, 5.7; 95% CI -2.8 to 14.2, P = 0.19) and judged the evidence 'not convincing', and the Noh et al. meta-analysis (42 studies involving 2625 participants) reported that its results failed to show acupuncture significantly more effective than placebo acupuncture in total UPDRS. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18618661/
- [statement] Appraisals of the acupuncture-for-PD literature rate its quality low: an overview of 11 systematic reviews and meta-analyses (Huang et al.) rated all included reviews very-low-quality on AMSTAR-2, with GRADE revealing 20 studies with very-low-quality evidence, 9 with low-quality evidence, 3 with moderate-quality evidence, and 0 with high-quality evidence, and its authors say their conclusion must be interpreted cautiously; the York CRD abstract of the Lee et al. review reports that seven RCTs were of low quality, and Noh et al. rated the methodological quality of their included RCTs low. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7482669/
- [statement] Evidence-quality statements on massage in PD are cautious: Kang et al. report approximately 42.9% low risk, 42.9% some concerns and 14.3% high risk of overall bias and note that complete blinding of participants and personnel was impossible; Angelopoulou et al. cite methodological concerns, say longitudinal studies are needed, and report that Yin Tui Na technique combined with acupuncture was associated with worse motor scores; and Parkinson's UK says research suggests massage may help to reduce pain, anxiety and depression, although there is no conclusive evidence. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9483027/

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/acupuncture-massage-and-traditional-adjuncts-in-pd/ · 15 claims from 10 sources

## Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD

Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of cannabis and cannabinoids in Parkinson's disease (PD), published 2022 to 2026, report that the evidence does not establish clinical benefit. Individual randomized trials of CBD/THC oils, CBD and nabilone are small and heterogeneous: the Colorado CBD/THC trial and the 2026 São Paulo cannabis-oil trial found no significant difference on their primary outcomes, while one nabilone trial reported a non-motor symptom difference. Reported adverse events include dizziness, confusion and irritability. Positive effects described in uncontrolled studies were not confirmed by small RCTs, per one review. The Parkinson's Foundation does not endorse use for PD symptoms or disease progression. One phase II CBD trial was listed as recruiting in the registry.

- [statement] As published, the Parkinson's Foundation consensus statement (May 2020) says that, given the lack of any clear data supporting the use of cannabis in PD, the Foundation does not endorse its use for PD symptoms or to modify disease progression; the Foundation's web page states that there is no conclusive evidence marijuana helps with PD symptoms; and a document hosted on the Michael J. Fox Foundation website, with content current to March 2022, states that controlled trials have not yet proven the safety or benefit of cannabis in Parkinson's. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinson.org/sites/default/files/documents/medical_cannabis_statement_finalv2_5.pdf
- [statement] Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of cannabis or cannabinoids in PD, published between 2022 and 2026, conclude that the evidence does not establish clinical benefit: Urbi et al. report that no compelling evidence was found to recommend the use of cannabis in PD patients, while also identifying a potential benefit with respect to alleviation of PD related tremor, anxiety, pain, improvement of sleep quality and quality of life; Messak et al. report that cannabinoids have not shown significant benefit in PD; Fernandes et al. report that current randomized evidence is insufficient to establish clinically meaningful benefits. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34958046/
- [statement] Positive findings on cannabis in PD come from open-label or uncontrolled designs that the sources treat with caution: a 2026 single-center open-label prospective cohort of 68 patients initiating medical cannabis reported improvements in the Non-Motor Symptoms Scale total score at 3 months, with a dropout rate of 26.5%, and its authors call the findings exploratory; an earlier systematic review states that positive effects described in uncontrolled studies have not been confirmed by the few and small RCTs; and the Parkinson's Foundation consensus statement says studies suggesting non-motor benefit are generally small, uncontrolled and open label, and that more rigorous research is needed. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42304702/
- [statement] The 2014 American Academy of Neurology systematic review of medical marijuana in selected neurologic disorders concluded that oral cannabis extract is probably ineffective for treating levodopa-induced dyskinesias in patients with Parkinson disease; the PubMed record title of this report carries the label [RETIRED], and the Parkinson's Foundation 2020 statement cites the same AAN conclusion. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24778283/
- [statement] Adverse-event findings reported for cannabinoids versus placebo in PD include: the Fernandes et al. meta-analysis of seven randomized trials reports increased risk of confusion (risk ratio, 4.44; 95% confidence interval, 1.17-16.87) and dizziness (risk ratio, 2.78; 95% confidence interval, 1.65-4.68); the Colorado CBD/THC trial reports twice as many treatment emergent adverse events in the CBD/THC group, most of them mild; and the São Paulo cannabis-oil trial reports irritability more frequent in the CBD/THC group (P = 0.005). (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42966680/

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/cannabis-and-cannabinoids-in-pd/ · 14 claims from 14 sources

## Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs

Group-based exercise modes in Parkinson's disease are described by guidelines and reviews with mixed strength. The APTA guideline gives community-based exercise a strong recommendation with high evidence strength, while the European guideline gives only weak recommendations for dance and a strong one for tai chi on UPDRS III. Randomized trials report better limits-of-stability with tai chi than resistance training or stretching and better MDS-UPDRS-3 with 12 months of tango than no intervention. Meta-analyses diverge on quality of life for tai chi and qigong, on yoga robustness, on Nordic walking benefit and on boxing, and review authors describe dance evidence as low certainty or critically low confidence.

- [statement] The APTA clinical practice guideline for physical therapist management of Parkinson disease states that physical therapists should recommend community-based exercise to reduce motor disease severity and improve nonmotor symptoms, functional outcomes, and quality of life, rating evidence strength as high and recommendation strength as strong. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/
- [statement] Review authors state quality limits on the dance literature: an umbrella review of 55 systematic reviews rated the overall confidence in the results of 38 reviews (69%) as critically low; a systematic review of 20 RCTs (N = 723) reported that small samples and methodological limitations resulted in low-certainty evidence across outcomes; and a systematic review of sixteen RCTs noted that performance bias cannot be controlled because participants and personnel cannot be blinded to a dance intervention and that less than half of the studies used a low-risk randomization procedure. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11687919/
- [statement] Adverse-event findings reported in the sources read: the APTA guideline reports that studies found no significant differences in adverse events between community-based exercise and the comparison groups, Li et al. observed no serious adverse events in their tai chi trial, and Ban et al. state that none of the included articles in their yoga meta-analysis reported serious adverse events. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/
- [statement] Meta-analytic findings on tai chi and qigong and quality of life in Parkinson's disease differ: Song et al. (15 RCTs) reported improved quality of life (ES=-0.393, p<.001), whereas a meta-analysis of seven systematic reviews (Fidan et al.) and a meta-analysis of thirteen RCTs of traditional Chinese exercises (Song et al., later version) reported no statistically significant quality-of-life effect. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5618798/
- [statement] On dance and motor symptom severity the sources differ: the European Physiotherapy Guideline (first edition, December 2014) gives a weak recommendation against using dance to improve movement functions (UPDRS III), whereas two meta-analyses of randomized trials (Ismail et al., 20 RCTs; Carapellotti et al., sixteen RCTs) report better MDS-UPDRS scores with dance than in non-dancers or no-intervention controls. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinsonnet.nl/app/uploads/sites/3/2019/11/eu_guideline_parkinson_guideline_for_pt_s1.pdf

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/dance-tai-chi-yoga-boxing-and-community-exercise-programs/ · 15 claims from 12 sources

## Exercise and physical therapy in PD

Guidelines read here (NICE NG71, the APTA physical therapist guideline and the German Society for Neurology guideline) include physiotherapy statements. APTA grades aerobic exercise, resistance training and balance training as high evidence quality with strong recommendations, and flexibility exercises as low and weak. A Cochrane network meta-analysis of 154 RCTs reported benefits for most exercise types, little evidence of differences between types, and confidence from moderate to very low. Sources differ on quality-of-life effects and on high versus moderate intensity, and the PD REHAB trial found no difference in its primary outcome for physiotherapy plus occupational therapy. Reviews describe follow-up evidence as short, and sources differ on whether exercise slows progression. SPARX3, a phase 3 high-intensity treadmill trial, was listed as active, not recruiting, with no results posted.

- [statement] For balance training the APTA clinical practice guideline states evidence quality high and recommendation strength strong; the Cochrane network meta-analysis reports that gait/balance/functional training probably has a moderate beneficial effect on the severity of motor signs (MD -7.50, 95% CI -11.39 to -3.48; moderate confidence; negative estimates reflect improvement); and a physiotherapy meta-analysis of 191 trials reports that balance and gait training, among other modalities, improved motor symptoms, balance, and gait. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/
- [statement] Reviews state that follow-up evidence is limited: the Cochrane physiotherapy review found benefit in most outcomes over the short term (less than 3 months), the aerobic exercise meta-analysis reported no valid evidence on follow-up effects, the physiotherapy meta-analysis by Radder and colleagues stated that it was not possible to perform a meta-analysis on long-term effects, and the Cochrane network meta-analysis analysed effects only up to six weeks after the intervention; the APTA guideline states that gains appear to dissipate if exercise is discontinued. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7120224/
- [statement] The APTA clinical practice guideline and the Cochrane network meta-analysis state different certainty ratings for aerobic (endurance) exercise and for resistance training: APTA labels both with high evidence quality and strong recommendation strength, while the Cochrane review rates confidence as low for endurance training and for strength/resistance training on the severity of motor signs. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/
- [statement] SPARX3 (NCT04284436) is a phase 3 multicenter randomized evaluator-blinded treadmill endurance-exercise trial in persons with PD diagnosed within 3 years and untreated with symptomatic therapy, comparing moderate intensity (60–65% of maximum heart rate) with high intensity (80–85%) at 4 days per week and 30 minutes per session, with change in the MDS-UPDRS motor score (Part III) over 12 months as the primary outcome. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9535216/
- [statement] Sources differ on whether exercise or physiotherapy improved quality of life: the APTA guideline, the Cochrane network meta-analysis (low confidence for gait/balance/functional training) and a large physiotherapy meta-analysis report quality-of-life improvements for some interventions, whereas the PD REHAB trial, the earlier Cochrane physiotherapy review and a meta-analysis of aerobic exercise report no significant quality-of-life difference. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/exercise-and-physical-therapy-in-pd/ · 15 claims from 9 sources

## LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy

LSVT LOUD and LSVT BIG are standardized, intensive programmes (16 sessions over four weeks) that train the amplitude of voice or limb movement. In the PD COMM trial of 388 people, LSVT LOUD lowered self-reported voice handicap versus no therapy and versus NHS speech and language therapy, with benefit still present at 12 months and mostly minor vocal-strain adverse events. Two Cochrane reviews (searches to April 2011) found insufficient evidence; later meta-analyses report higher vocal loudness, while intelligibility results are mixed. NICE NG71 recommends speech and language therapy including attention to effort therapies; RCSLT guidance (December 2025) highly recommends LSVT LOUD. For LSVT BIG, the Berlin trial reported UPDRS motor gains, but a meta-analysis found only trends for walking and rated evidence preliminary.

- [statement] A review by LSVT researchers, two of whom disclose ownership interest in LSVT Global, Inc., tabulates LSVT LOUD and LSVT BIG as standardized protocols with a dosage of 4 consecutive days a week for 4 weeks (16 sessions in one month); the PD COMM trial likewise delivered LSVT LOUD as four sessions each week over four weeks. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3316992/
- [statement] In a published comparison table of the two programmes, LSVT LOUD directs increased movement amplitude predominately to the respiratory/laryngeal systems whereas LSVT BIG directs it across the limb motor system including gait; the Berlin LSVT BIG study report describes LSVT BIG as focusing on intensive exercising of high-amplitude movements. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3316992/
- [statement] NICE guideline NG71, published 19 July 2017 and last reviewed 19 December 2024, recommends offering speech and language therapy to people with Parkinson's disease who are experiencing problems with communication, swallowing or saliva (recommendation 1.7.8), including strategies to improve speech and communication 'such as attention to effort therapies'; Parkinson's UK's summary of the NICE guideline and the Canadian guideline for Parkinson disease (which grades the recommendation A and cites NICE as its source) restate it. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/Recommendations
- [statement] The PD COMM pilot trial reported a trend to improvement in the Voice Handicap Index at three months with both LSVT LOUD and standard speech and language therapy versus control, whereas the full PD COMM trial reported benefit for LSVT LOUD but no evidence of benefit for NHS speech and language therapy versus no therapy. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5763537/
- [statement] In PD COMM, the Voice Handicap Index total score remained lower with LSVT LOUD than with no speech and language therapy at six months (-7.2; 99% confidence interval -13.3 to -1.1) and at 12 months (-6.7; -12.6 to -0.8); the authors write that re-intervention might still be required should the treatment effect wear off or as Parkinson's disease progresses. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11232530/

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/lsvt-big-lsvt-loud-and-speech-language-therapy/ · 17 claims from 12 sources

## Music, art and creative therapies in PD

Educational summary of what published sources say, not medical advice. Meta-analyses of rhythmic auditory stimulation and music-based interventions in Parkinson's disease report positive pooled effects on gait velocity and stride length but not cadence, and disagree on balance, timed up-and-go, UPDRS motor scores and freezing of gait. One singing review rates the certainty of its RCT-based finding as very low and another calls singing a promising adjunct therapy, and a trial's own authors limit attribution to singing. Reviews conflict on quality of life, mood and cognition. The visual art therapy evidence cited here is an exploratory observational study, and a meta-analysis calls visual arts and painting a research gap; one art-therapy meta-analysis of 26 trials included 14 dance trials. Review authors repeatedly flag small samples and limited blinding.

- [statement] Five systematic reviews with meta-analysis of rhythmic auditory cueing, rhythmic auditory stimulation (RAS) or music-based interventions in Parkinson's disease (Ghai, Ye, Wang, Lee and Ko, and Li) each report a positive pooled effect on gait velocity or speed and on stride or step length. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5764963/
- [statement] The Ye, Wang, Lee and Ko, and Li meta-analyses each report no statistically significant pooled effect of RAS or music-based interventions on cadence in Parkinson's disease. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9366143/
- [statement] Meta-analyses differ on UPDRS motor scores and freezing of gait for music-based therapy and RAS in Parkinson's disease: one meta-analysis (K = 6 studies, total N = 168) found no significant effects for UPDRS-motor score or Freezing of Gait, whereas Ye and colleagues (18 studies) report significant pooled improvements in UPDRS-III and in the Freezing of Gait Questionnaire. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22166406/
- [statement] Meta-analyses of RAS and music-based interventions in Parkinson's disease differ on balance and timed up-and-go (TUG) mobility: Wang and colleagues and Lee and Ko report statistically significant pooled improvements (Berg Balance Scale and TUG for Wang and colleagues; TUG for Lee and Ko), whereas Ye and colleagues report no significant pooled difference for either, and Li and colleagues report a pooled balance effect that became nonsignificant after sensitivity analysis. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9053573/
- [statement] Two recent systematic reviews of singing in Parkinson's disease word their conclusions differently: Irons and Sheffield (23 studies, 540 participants; last search 3 April 2025) rate the certainty of the one RCT-based favourable outcome as very low and state that, due to insufficient high-quality evidence, they are unable to determine the effects of singing interventions, whereas Trinchillo and colleagues (twenty-six studies, 1057 patients; considerable heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis) conclude that singing is a promising adjunct therapy. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645629/

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/music-art-and-creative-therapies-in-pd/ · 14 claims from 12 sources

## Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training

What published sources report about occupational therapy, external cueing and gait training in Parkinson's disease. NICE guideline NG71 and an AOTA practice guideline address occupational therapy. The OTiP trial reported a favourable primary outcome, the PD REHAB trial reported no difference on its primary outcome, and a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence. The APTA guideline rates external cueing and gait training as high evidence quality with strong recommendation strength, yet meta-analyses differ on the best cue modality, and a 2026 meta-analysis found no significant reduction in freezing-of-gait severity. Treadmill meta-analyses report improved walking speed but not cadence. Authors describe cueing durability as unclear and wearable cueing as evaluated mainly in laboratories. This is an attributed summary of sources, not medical advice.

- [statement] Sources describe limited durability of cueing effects: the APTA guideline states that the lasting effects of cueing are unclear because benefits appear to dissipate over time, and that effects appear to dissipate when the cues are removed; the RESCUE crossover trial (153 patients; 3-week home cueing programme using a prototype cueing device) reported that effects of intervention had reduced considerably at 6-week follow-up; and a narrative review of cueing in people with freezing of gait reported that long-term consolidation and transfer of the effects appear to be hampered in that subgroup. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/
- [statement] Two meta-analyses report improved walking speed with treadmill training in Parkinson's disease but no improvement in cadence: the Cochrane review (18 trials, 633 participants; last searched September 2014) reported improved gait speed (MD = 0.09 m/s; 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.03 to 0.14; moderate quality of evidence) and that cadence did not improve (MD = 2.16 steps/minute; 95% CI -0.13 to 4.46; low quality of evidence), and a second meta-analysis (16 trials across Parkinson's disease and multiple sclerosis) reported improved comfortable walking velocity in Parkinson's disease (MD 0.21m/second, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.27) and that treadmill training had no effect on cadence. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9579750/
- [statement] Three sources include cueing among their gait recommendations: the APTA clinical practice guideline states that physical therapists should implement external cueing to reduce motor disease severity and freezing of gait (FOG) and to improve gait outcomes in individuals with Parkinson disease (evidence quality: high; recommendation strength: strong), with aggregate evidence of thirteen high-quality and 16 moderate-quality studies; Keus et al. extracted cueing strategies to improve gait as one of four treatment recommendations based on evidence from more than two controlled trials; and a 2020 systematic review of physical therapy for FOG and gait impairments reports that cueing strategies (visual and auditory) reduce FOG with a good category A recommendation. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/
- [statement] A Cochrane review of occupational therapy for Parkinson's disease, with electronic searches up to April 2007, identified two trials with 84 patients in total, and its authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to support or refute the efficacy of occupational therapy in Parkinson's disease; the PD REHAB report describes Cochrane reviews of physiotherapy and occupational therapy for Parkinson's disease as having found insufficient evidence of effectiveness. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6991932/
- [statement] On technology-delivered cueing, a technological review of wearable cueing systems for freezing of gait states that novel cueing systems have been evaluated predominantly in laboratory settings, a narrative review states that the increasing use of wearable technology is allowing the cue type, cue content and dose to be adapted to individual patients, and the APTA guideline notes that the cost of utilizing technology for the external cueing source should be considered. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6470562/

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/occupational-therapy-cueing-and-gait-training/ · 15 claims from 9 sources

## Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants

Trial evidence for supplements and failed neuroprotectants in Parkinson disease is largely negative in the sources read. Large trials of coenzyme Q10 (QE3), creatine (NET-PD LS-1), inosine (SURE-PD3) and isradipine (STEADY-PD III) each reported no clinical benefit, as did a tocopherol trial. Earlier signals, a CoQ10 dosage-ranging trial reporting a positive trend and a creatine futility screen that did not reject it, were followed by later large trials reporting no benefit. Vitamin D reports are mixed. Mucuna pruriens trials are small and short, and commercial products varied widely from labelled levodopa. NICE NG71 recommends against vitamin E and, except in the context of clinical trials, against co-enzyme Q10 as neuroprotective therapy, recommends that creatine supplements not be offered, and advises a vitamin D supplement. This summarizes what sources report; it is not medical advice.

- [statement] In a randomized trial of tocopherol (a component of vitamin E) and deprenyl in early Parkinson's disease (800 patients assigned to placebo, tocopherol, deprenyl or both; N Engl J Med 1993), there was no beneficial effect of tocopherol or any interaction between tocopherol and deprenyl, and a 2026 review likewise reports that no benefits of vitamin E were seen in UPDRS total score. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8417384/
- [statement] Two published meta-analyses of randomized trials of coenzyme Q10 in Parkinson disease reported no significant benefit over placebo: a 2016 analysis of five RCTs (981 patients) found that the overall effect did not favor either group for total UPDRS, and a 2017 analysis of eight studies (899 patients) found a pooled WMD of 1.02 for UPDRS part 3 (p = 0.54) and stated that routine CoQ10 treatment of PD could not be recommended. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26553164/
- [statement] In the NINDS NET-PD program, a randomized phase II futility trial of creatine and minocycline (Neurology 2006) found that neither could be rejected as futile and recommended considering both for definitive phase III trials, whereas the later Long-term Study 1 of creatine monohydrate 10 g/d (JAMA 2015; 1741 participants) was terminated early for futility at a planned interim analysis (n = 955) and concluded that creatine did not improve clinical outcomes. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16481597/
- [statement] Two analyses of commercial Mucuna pruriens products reported wide variation in levodopa content: a 2018 HPLC analysis of six products found levodopa content varying from 6% to 141% of label claims with no product within the 90%–110% pharmacopeial limits, and a 2022 JAMA Neurology case series of 16 analyzed supplements found 15 containing levodopa at 2 mg to 241 mg per recommended serving, with actual levodopa 228% to 2186% greater than the estimate for products listing a seed-extract quantity, while carbidopa and benserazide were not detected. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5808387/
- [statement] A 2014 Cochrane review (searches to 10 November 2013; two RCTs, 194 patients) reported no clear evidence of an effect of creatine on motor function (MD -0.26; 95% CI -4.39 to 3.88; low quality evidence) and judged the evidence base limited by risk of bias, small sample sizes and short duration, and a 2017 BMC Neurology meta-analysis (five RCTs, 1339 participants) reported no significant differences in total, mental, activities of daily living or motor UPDRS scores, with an improvement in Schwab & England Scale scores, and concluded that creatine has no observed benefit in PD. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10196714/

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/supplements-coq10-creatine-vitamin-d-mucuna-and-failed-neuroprotectants/ · 14 claims from 13 sources

# Surgical and device therapies
Source: https://llmsx.org/tree/parkinson-s-disease-surgical-and-device-therapies-deep-brain-stimulation-adaptive-dbs-focused-ultrasound-levodopa-pumps-and-infusions-and-neuromodulation-for-gait/

> Surgical and device therapies: deep brain stimulation, adaptive DBS, focused ultrasound, levodopa pumps and infusions, and neuromodulation for gait. 5 concept packs; the section's 94 claims are in llms-facts.txt#parkinson-s-disease-surgical-and-device-therapies-deep-brain-stimulation-adaptive-dbs-focused-ultrasound-levodopa-pumps-and-infusions-and-neuromodulation-for-gait.

## Adaptive closed-loop DBS and directional leads

Adaptive DBS uses neural feedback to adjust stimulation; directional leads steer the stimulation field. These approaches address different programming dimensions. Personalized adaptive DBS showed benefits in a small feasibility trial, while another small beta-feedback trial found no significant advantage over continuous DBS. ADAPT-PD supported long-term tolerability and preserved therapeutic performance with important open-label design limits. Directional stimulation widened the therapeutic window in a randomized crossover study, but a separate randomized trial did not demonstrate superior motor outcomes. Algorithm, biomarker, endpoint, and programming differences matter when interpreting results.

- [statement] Adaptive DBS adjusts stimulation amplitude using neural feedback; the beta-band dual-threshold approach adjusts amplitude according to subthalamic local-field-potential power. (high confidence) — https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-roundup-february-28-2025
- [statement] FDA's PMA database record for Medtronic supplement P960009/S478 (Activa, Percept and SenSight Deep Brain Stimulation Therapy System) lists a decision date of 02/20/2025 and an approval order statement for a new optional programming feature called adaptive deep brain stimulation (aDBS), within the indication of adjunctive therapy for levodopa-responsive Parkinson's disease of at least 4 years' duration that is not adequately controlled with medication. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfpma/pma.cfm?id=P960009S478
- [statement] The FDA summary of safety and effectiveness for P960009/S478 states that the aDBS feature has been marketed for Parkinson's disease in Japan with the Percept PC since May 2020 and the Percept RC since November 2022, and in Europe with both models since January 2025. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cdrh_docs/pdf/P960009S478B.pdf
- [statement] A nine-patient double-blind randomized crossover trial using consecutive one-month treatment periods and beta-band dual-threshold control reported no statistically significant adaptive-versus-continuous DBS differences; the authors reported between-patient heterogeneity and called for adequately powered follow-up. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42765432/
- [statement] The FDA summary of safety and effectiveness for P960009/S478 states that aDBS was not studied in the ADAPT-PD trial with bilaterally implanted neurostimulators, that only subjects with single implanted neurostimulators were eligible, and that the labeling instructs clinicians not to use aDBS with more than one implanted neurostimulator. (low confidence) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cdrh_docs/pdf/P960009S478B.pdf

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/adaptive-closed-loop-dbs-and-directional-leads/ · 14 claims from 9 sources

## Deep brain stimulation (STN/GPi): patient selection and programming

STN and GPi DBS selection depends on the patient’s disabling symptoms, levodopa response, neuropsychological risks and treatment goals. Both targets can improve motor symptoms; medication-reduction goals favor STN, while selected dyskinesia and cognitive or mood concerns can favor GPi. Interdisciplinary evaluation and realistic expectations are central. Programming uses contact testing and adjustment of amplitude, pulse width and frequency, supported by device checks and coordinated medication management. Comparative cognitive findings depend on the study and stimulation setting, and axial symptoms require separate counseling.

- [statement] For conventional ring-contact programming, monopolar review tests contacts individually with the lead contact as cathode and pulse-generator case as anode, identifying benefit and adverse-effect thresholds to select a therapeutic window. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6558426/
- [statement] For candidates with substantial concern about cognitive decline or depression, the CNS guideline advises considering GPi over STN while weighing the other goals of surgery; this is risk-based selection, not a guarantee of cognitive or mood safety. (medium confidence) — https://www.cns.org/guidelines/congress-of-neurological-surgeons-systematic-revie/
- [statement] Conventional initial monopolar testing commonly holds pulse width at 60 μs and frequency at 130 Hz while amplitude is increased to identify benefit and side-effect thresholds. These are starting settings described in programming literature, not a universal prescription. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6558426/
- [statement] When medication reduction is not anticipated and suppressing on-medication dyskinesia is the goal, the CNS guideline favors GPi; GPi can have a direct antidyskinetic effect while medication is maintained. (medium confidence) — https://www.cns.org/guidelines/congress-of-neurological-surgeons-systematic-revie/
- [statement] When substantial dopaminergic medication reduction is the main surgical goal, evidence and the CNS guideline favor STN over GPi; medication reduction remains an individualized objective. (medium confidence) — https://www.cns.org/guidelines/congress-of-neurological-surgeons-systematic-revie/

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/deep-brain-stimulation-stn-gpi-patient-selection-and-programming/ · 21 claims from 9 sources

## Device-aided therapies compared: pumps, infusions and DBS

Device-aided therapies address disabling motor fluctuations inadequately controlled by oral treatment. Subcutaneous apomorphine and levodopa pumps, intestinal levodopa infusion and DBS differ in invasiveness, daily management and adverse effects. Comparative cohorts and indirect meta-analyses suggest benefits but cannot establish a universal winner because selection and baseline differences matter.
