Hoehn–Yahr describes motor disability, especially laterality, balance and physical independence. Braak staging describes a proposed sequence of postmortem α-synuclein pathology; exceptions limit its interpretation as a universal course or clinical severity measure. SynNeurGe combines synuclein pathology, neurodegeneration and genetics with clinical manifestations for research classification. Its authors explicitly refrained from proposing a temporal staging sequence, distinguishing it from NSD-ISS. These frameworks answer different questions and should be identified by name when comparing research populations. The NSD-ISS has been applied to PPMI, PASADENA and SPARK data.

- [statement] SynNeurGe’s proposed biological classification has three components: pathological α-synuclein in tissues or CSF (S), imaging evidence of neurodegeneration (N), and pathogenic variants that cause or strongly predispose to Parkinson’s disease (G). (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38267191/
- [statement] Braak staging proposes a neuropathological sequence beginning in lower-brainstem or olfactory structures, proceeding toward substantia nigra involvement and eventually cortex; the proposed direction of spread is a hypothesis rather than a clinical disability score. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2605160/
- [statement] The Braak pathological sequence is not universal across patients or Lewy-body disorders; reviews describe nonconforming distributions, so it should not be assumed to represent every patient’s disease course. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2605160/
- [statement] Braak’s proposed pattern does not apply to every patient: the 2017 review limits its staging fit to a subset with young onset and long disease duration, while the 2008 critical evaluation reports exceptions and neurologically intact people with extensive postmortem pathology. (medium confidence) — https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neurology/articles/10.3389/fneur.2017.00037/full
- [statement] SynNeurGe classifies pathological α-synuclein (S), neurodegeneration (N), and pathogenic genetic variants (G), linked to clinical manifestations (C); these are biological classification dimensions. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38267191/

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/pd-staging-hoehn-yahr-braak-and-biological-synneurge/ · 19 claims from 9 sources

## Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction

Prodromal PD research estimates disease probability before classic motor diagnosis by combining age and risk-marker information. Polysomnography-confirmed isolated REM sleep behaviour disorder is a strong marker, but its phenoconversion outcomes include dementia and other disorders as well as PD. Hyposmia is associated with increased subsequent PD risk yet has limited specificity. Cohort conversion percentages, relative risks and Bayesian prodromal probabilities describe different quantities and should not be substituted for an individual forecast. The MDS research framework and its 2019 update support research stratification; the 2019 multicentre RBD study, 2024 Mayo cohort and 2024 Lifelines analysis demonstrate why population, ascertainment, marker availability and follow-up matter.

- [statement] Prodromal PD describes early symptoms or signs of neurodegeneration before fully evolved motor parkinsonism permits a classic clinical diagnosis; the original MDS prodromal criteria were explicitly developed for research purposes only. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26474317/
- [statement] Isolated RBD involves dream enactment and loss of normal REM sleep atonia in the absence of an established neurodegenerative disorder. The cited risk cohorts used polysomnography-confirmed RBD; their estimates should not be assigned to questionnaire-positive dream enactment alone. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6391615/
- [statement] The MDS research framework combines an age-based prior probability with marker likelihood ratios in a Bayesian naïve classifier; probable prodromal PD means at least 80% estimated certainty that prodromal disease is present, rather than an 80% prediction of clinical conversion within a specified number of years. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26474317/
- [statement] Smell loss alone has limited specificity: it can occur in neurological diseases other than PD. The hyposmia meta-analysis explicitly cautioned that the limited evidence did not establish hyposmia as a solid stand-alone predictor of PD. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6545790/
- [statement] Isolated RBD is a strong prodromal marker for a spectrum of neurodegenerative outcomes, including Parkinson’s disease, dementia with Lewy bodies and multiple system atrophy; a reported overall phenoconversion rate is therefore not a PD-only conversion rate. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6391615/

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/prodromal-pd-rbd-hyposmia-and-risk-prediction/ · 13 claims from 6 sources

# Frontier platforms
Source: https://llmsx.org/tree/parkinson-s-disease-frontier-platforms-cell-replacement-gene-therapy-digital-biomarkers-ai-gut-brain-axis-and-precision-medicine/

> Frontier platforms: dopaminergic cell replacement, gene therapy, digital biomarkers and wearables, AI, the gut-brain axis with body-first versus brain-first subtypes, and precision medicine. 6 concept packs; the section's 28 claims are in llms-facts.txt#parkinson-s-disease-frontier-platforms-cell-replacement-gene-therapy-digital-biomarkers-ai-gut-brain-axis-and-precision-medicine.

## AI and machine learning in PD diagnosis and progression

Systematic reviews of machine learning in Parkinson's disease report a translation gap: very few systems have been adopted for real-world use, external validation is uncommon and accuracy is lower on external test sets, and data leakage is associated with inflated accuracy. The reviews also report high headline accuracy alongside low-quality evidence and a high risk of bias in most assessed studies, and a preprint reports that subject-aware splitting lowers reported performance. A machine learning study of longitudinal clinical data reports projections of progression and a replication in an independent cohort. The reviews' proportions describe the samples assessed, not the whole literature.

- [statement] The biomarker review states that its proportions describe the sample assessed, not the entire PD machine learning literature, and an earlier review likewise describes its work as sampling current ML practices in PD applications. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13702696/
- [statement] One review cites a UK autopsy study that found the misdiagnosis rate of PD is 24%, and a neuroimaging review states that the heterogeneous disease phenotype and overlapping symptoms with atypical parkinsonian syndromes (APS) contribute to high misdiagnosis rates. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11112052/
- [statement] Systematic reviews of machine learning in PD report a translation gap: one states that very few ML systems have been adopted for real-world use despite the large number of studies published every year, and a later review concludes that reported performance has advanced faster than evidence of generalizability and clinical implementation. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11112052/
- [statement] External validation is uncommon in the reviewed literature: the neuroimaging review reports that very few studies employed external test sets (8%), where accuracy was significantly lower, and the later biomarker review reports that only 20 (7.6%) of the studies met its external-validation definition and that in ten within-study comparisons external performance fell in eight. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11657025/
- [statement] High reported accuracy coexists with weak evidence quality: a gait meta-analysis states that its GRADE analysis revealed low-quality evidence for precision and F1 score and very-low quality for accuracy, specificity, and sensitivity, and the biomarker review reports median best-model accuracy of 95.3% while 259 studies (98.1%) were at high overall risk of bias under its adapted PROBAST rules. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13362068/

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/ai-and-machine-learning-in-pd-diagnosis-and-progression/ · 13 claims from 7 sources

## Digital biomarkers: wearables and remote monitoring in PD

Wearable sensors, smartwatches and smartphone apps are studied as digital measures of Parkinson's disease for early detection, longitudinal change and regulatory endpoints. A UK Biobank accelerometry analysis reports better test performance for prodromal disease than models based on genetics, lifestyle, blood biochemistry or prodromal symptoms, and the multicenter WATCH-PD observational study reports device-derived features that differed between early Parkinson's disease and age-matched controls. Reviews report that most included studies were cross-sectional and call for standardization. A systematic review reports that no real-world walking speed measure has been fully validated by the FDA, and that a stride velocity endpoint approved by the EMA concerns a different disease. Consensus experts name the lack of clear reference values as the main challenge for digital mobility outcomes.

- [statement] Four reviews each point to standardization needs: a Movement Disorders systematic review of early Parkinson's disease calls for standardized study methodologies, a scoping review of prodromal Parkinson's disease says future research should prioritize standardized assessment, a real-world walking speed review says adoption requires improved standardization of devices, algorithms, and study methodologies, and a review of digital biomarkers for precision diagnosis and monitoring notes a lack of standardized data verification protocols. (high confidence) — https://movementdisorders.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mds.30056
- [statement] The 95th centile of stride velocity has been approved by the EMA as a primary endpoint for assessing ambulant patients with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy, a regulatory precedent in a disease other than Parkinson's disease. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-02-17) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12954611/
- [statement] WATCH-PD was a 12-month, multicenter observational study in which 82 individuals with early, untreated PD and 50 age-matched controls wore research-grade sensors, a smartwatch, and a smartphone while performing standardized assessments in the clinic. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108794/
- [statement] A scoping review of prodromal Parkinson's disease and a systematic review of wearable sensors for early diagnosis each report that most included studies were cross-sectional. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13697243/
- [statement] A three-round consensus study of 12 experts from the Mobilise-D consortium’s Parkinson’s Disease Working Group reached full consensus on a clinical utility framework for digital mobility outcomes with three main categories. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12447593/

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/digital-biomarkers-wearables-and-remote-monitoring-in-pd/ · 13 claims from 8 sources

## Dopaminergic cell replacement: bemdaneprocel and iPSC-derived neurons

Cell replacement for Parkinson's disease transplants dopaminergic progenitor cells derived from embryonic or induced pluripotent stem cells. Recent early-phase, open-label trials of an embryonic stem cell product and an induced pluripotent stem cell product report safety findings plus exploratory motor and imaging changes, and their authors caution about small cohorts, the absence of a control group and placebo effects. In one trial the authors state that risks were primarily associated with the immunosuppression regimen. A randomized, sham surgery-controlled phase three trial of the embryonic stem cell product is registered as recruiting, and a sponsor announced a conditional, time-limited approval in Japan of an induced pluripotent stem cell product.

- [statement] In the bemdaneprocel phase I trial, twelve patients were enrolled sequentially in a low-dose cohort of 0.9 million cells and a high-dose cohort of 2.7 million cells, and all of the participants received one year of immunosuppression. (medium confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-08845-y
- [statement] Sumitomo Pharma announced that, as of March 6, 2026, it obtained conditional and time-limited approval in Japan for the allogeneic iPS cell-derived dopaminergic neural progenitor cell product AMCHEPRY (INN: raguneprocel). (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-03-11) — https://www.sumitomo-pharma.com/news/20260306.html
- [statement] The registry record lists exPDite-2 as RECRUITING with an estimated primary completion date of 2028-10, and the sponsor-authored abstract states that the first participant was randomized and underwent surgery in August 2025. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-02) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT06944522
- [statement] The registry describes exPDite-2 as a Phase 3 multicenter, randomized, sham surgery-controlled, double-blind study in approximately 102 adults with Parkinson's disease, with participants randomized in a 2:1 ratio to receive bemdaneprocel or undergo sham surgery. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-02) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT06944522
- [statement] The bemdaneprocel authors caution that their data need to be interpreted cautiously in view of the open-label study design, the small patient cohort, the relatively short observation period, the expected fluctuations in PD symptoms and the possibility of placebo effects; the registry lists the study as a single group with no masking. (medium confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-08845-y

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/dopaminergic-cell-replacement-bemdaneprocel-and-ipsc-derived-neurons/ · 13 claims from 5 sources

## Gene therapy in PD: AAV-GDNF/AADC/GAD and GBA1 vectors

Gene therapy for Parkinson's disease uses adeno-associated viral vectors that carry genes such as GDNF, AADC, GAD and neurturin, and, in registered programmes, GBA1. The early-phase GDNF study reports safety findings and exploratory motor changes, and its authors state that a randomized controlled study is planned to confirm them. In a sham-controlled GAD trial the scores fell in both arms, with a greater fall in the gene therapy arm, while a sham-controlled neurturin trial was not superior to sham surgery. A randomized, sham-controlled GDNF study is registered, and a registry record for an intravenous GBA1 programme is withdrawn. A regulator announcement about AADC deficiency concerns a different indication.

- [statement] REGENERATE-PD (NCT06285643) is registered as a phase 2 randomized, double-blind, sham surgery-controlled study of intraputaminal AAV2-GDNF in adults with moderate stage Parkinson's disease. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-05) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT06285643
- [statement] The phase 1b trial NCT04167540 of AAV2-GDNF (AB-1005) enrolled 11 participants, 5 in the Mild Cohort and 6 in the Moderate Cohort, per the authors' abstract and the registry record. (medium confidence) — https://www.neurology.org/doi/10.1212/WNL.0000000000206690
- [statement] In the phase 2 randomised trial of bilateral AAV2-GAD delivery in the subthalamic nucleus in advanced Parkinson's disease, the primary outcome measure was the 6-month change from baseline in double-blind assessment of off-medication UPDRS motor scores. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21419704/
- [statement] The registry record for REGENERATE-PD (NCT06285643) lists a primary outcome of change from baseline to Month 18 on PD Motor Diary (normalized Good ON time per Hauser Diary), an actual enrollment of 59, and the status ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-05) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT06285643
- [statement] At 18 months post-treatment the authors report improvements from baseline in the Moderate Cohort in mean±SE MDS-UPDRS Part III OFF scores (−18.8±6.6), describe possible clinical benefit, and state that a phase 2 randomized controlled study is planned to confirm these findings. (low confidence) — https://www.neurology.org/doi/10.1212/WNL.0000000000206690

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/gene-therapy-in-pd-aav-gdnf-aadc-gad-and-gba1-vectors/ · 13 claims from 9 sources

## Gut-brain axis: microbiome and body-first versus brain-first PD

The brain-first versus body-first model proposes that alpha-synuclein pathology in Parkinson's disease begins either in the brain or in the enteric or peripheral autonomic nervous system, and the proposers hypothesize that isolated REM sleep behaviour disorder is a prodromal phenotype of the body-first type. In their own review the proposers report that molecular imaging studies were generally in agreement with the model whereas structural imaging studies showed conflicting findings, a commentary notes limits on generalizability, and an autopsy preprint reports gut-restricted positivity in only a few subjects. Meta-analyses report gut microbiome alterations in Parkinson's disease, the authors of one state that differences in microbiome structure are small, and a later meta-analysis states that causality cannot be established. Two randomized fecal microbiota transplantation trials report different primary-outcome results.

- [statement] The authors of the original case-control study hypothesize that isolated REM sleep behaviour disorder (iRBD) is a prodromal phenotype for the body-first type, and a later longitudinal study states that the presence of rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (RBD) may be indicative of a body-first pattern. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32830221/
- [statement] In the brain-first versus body-first model, brain-first Parkinson's disease has α-synuclein pathology initially arising in the brain and spreading to the peripheral autonomic nervous system, while body-first Parkinson's disease has pathology originating in the enteric or peripheral autonomic nervous system and then spreading to the brain. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32830221/
- [statement] One meta-analysis reports that differences in microbiome structure between PD and controls are small, and a later meta-analysis states that causality cannot be established from predominantly observational studies. (medium confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-021-00156-z
- [statement] Two meta-analyses of PD gut microbiome studies report depletion of short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria, including Faecalibacterium and Lachnospiraceae, and enrichment of Akkermansia. (medium confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-021-00156-z
- [statement] The GUT-PARFECT paper title describes a phase 2 trial, whereas the registry record NCT03808389 lists phase NA, with the record status verified 2023-01. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2024-03-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11056595/

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/gut-brain-axis-microbiome-and-body-first-versus-brain-first-pd/ · 13 claims from 10 sources

## PD subtypes and precision medicine

Studies in different cohorts report that Parkinson's disease subtypes differ in progression, and authors link the failure of disease-modifying trials in part to heterogeneity. Published schemes include data-driven clusters and the SynNeurGe research classification, which combines pathological alpha-synuclein, neurodegeneration defined by neuroimaging and pathogenic gene variants. Authors report that replication of published subtype classifications is limited. A genetic consortium preprint reports many potentially trial-eligible carriers of GBA1 and LRRK2 variants. Sponsors state that the LRRK2 kinase inhibitor BIIB122 did not meet its endpoints in an early-stage study that included people with or without a pathogenic LRRK2 variant and that they will discontinue development in idiopathic disease, while a study in carriers continues. Reports differ on motor progression in seed amplification assay negative disease.

- [statement] The sponsors state that LUMA included individuals with early-stage Parkinson's disease with or without a pathogenic LRRK2 variant, and a foundation news article states that the trial largely included patients without known genetic mutations. (medium confidence) — https://investors.biogen.com/news-releases/news-release-details/biogen-and-denali-therapeutics-provide-update-phase-2b-luma
- [statement] After LUMA, Biogen and Denali state they will discontinue further development of BIIB122 in idiopathic Parkinson's disease, while Denali continues the Phase 2a BEACON study in carriers of a pathogenic LRRK2 variant. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-05-22) — https://investors.biogen.com/news-releases/news-release-details/biogen-and-denali-therapeutics-provide-update-phase-2b-luma
- [statement] Authors report that replication of published PD subtype classifications is limited: a Delphi-panel replication of eight data-driven systems found none reproducible in LABS-PD, and a separate validation study states that replication studies in independent cohorts are currently lacking. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30056038/
- [statement] Authors of two papers link the failure of disease-modifying trials in PD in part to heterogeneity, with one noting that negative trials treated all PD patients as a single homogenous group. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7483040/
- [statement] Studies in different cohorts report that Parkinson's disease subtypes differ in progression: one reports clusters associated with motor progression rates, another reports faster two-year progression in diffuse-malignant patients, and a third reports that data-driven subtypes exhibited the highest progression rates. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6288789/

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/pd-subtypes-and-precision-medicine/ · 13 claims from 10 sources

# Research ecosystem and health systems
Source: https://llmsx.org/tree/parkinson-s-disease-research-ecosystem-and-health-systems-trial-design-regulatory-pathways-registries-global-burden-and-care-access/

> Research ecosystem and health systems: clinical trial design and endpoints, regulatory pathways at FDA and EMA, patient registries and research participation, global burden, cost and access to care. 4 concept packs; the section's 171 claims are in llms-facts.txt#parkinson-s-disease-research-ecosystem-and-health-systems-trial-design-regulatory-pathways-registries-global-burden-and-care-access.

## Clinical trial design: endpoints, enrichment and platform trials in PD

Parkinson’s trial design separates symptomatic improvement from sustained changes in disease progression. Clinical scales, patient-relevant milestones and carefully defined enrichment strategies serve different purposes. The cited studies illustrate why wash-out and delayed-start findings need cautious interpretation, why clinically important change thresholds depend on the instrument and study method, and why imaging enrichment does not establish a surrogate endpoint. The platform trial combines interim treatment decisions with a registered combined rating-scale primary outcome.

- [statement] The same EMA questions-and-answers document states that, because L-dopa is increasingly given as initial treatment, the start of L-dopa therapy is no longer an optimal demarcation criterion between early and more advanced Parkinson’s disease. (low confidence) — https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/questions-and-answers-additional-clarification-inclusion-criteria-guideline-clinical-investigation-medicinal-products-treatment-parkinsons-disease-revision-2_en.pdf
- [statement] The EMA Parkinson’s guideline states that for early untreated Parkinson’s disease the goal is to slow progression of motor symptoms by assessing change in UPDRS, or time to L-Dopa+/DA-agonists, with a trial duration probably up to 24 months. (low confidence) — https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/guideline-clinical-investigation-medicinal-products-treatment-parkinsons-disease_en.pdf-0
- [statement] Foltynie and colleagues describe MDS UPDRS Part 1 as capturing non-motor symptoms, Part 2 as capturing motor impact on daily living, Part 3 as clinician-assessed motor severity, and Part 4 as motor complications. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-02-08) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13438061/
- [statement] UCL’s EJS ACT-PD news item states that participants have been randomised to telmisartan, terazosin or a matched placebo, and that the trial is expanding to test ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) as a third potential treatment. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-04) — https://www.innovative-ctu.ucl.ac.uk/news/news-stories/2026/november-2026/parkinson-s-trial-ejs-act-pd-adds-a-new-treatment-arm/
- [statement] The EMA Parkinson’s guideline describes improvement of the core symptoms, motor symptoms and activities of daily living, as the endpoint for adjunctive treatment in patients on L-Dopa+ with insufficient control of motor symptoms. (low confidence) — https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/guideline-clinical-investigation-medicinal-products-treatment-parkinsons-disease_en.pdf-0

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/clinical-trial-design-endpoints-enrichment-and-platform-trials-in-pd/ · 18 claims from 12 sources

## Global burden, economic cost and access to PD care

This concept connects estimates of the global Parkinson disease burden with economic costs and access to treatment. WHO and Global Burden of Disease analyses describe substantial populations living with the condition; the BMJ study models future prevalence. The economic studies quantify societal costs in the United States, with the later report covering both Parkinson disease and atypical parkinsonism. WHO describes barriers to medicine access, while studies of African essential medicines lists, Nigerian pharmacies and Middle Eastern physicians examine different aspects of access. Listing a medicine does not guarantee access, and physician perceptions do not substitute for objectively verified availability. Estimates remain attributed to their own studies, populations and methods.

- [statement] The Middle East survey authors caution that their data were physician-reported perceptions rather than objective verification, with potential reporting bias and failure to capture within-country variability. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-07-08) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13380763/
- [statement] The Global Burden of Disease collaborators estimated 6·1 million individuals with Parkinson disease globally in 2016, with a 95% uncertainty interval of 5·0–7·3 million. (low confidence) (verified as of 2018-11-01) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6191528/
- [statement] Fothergill-Misbah and colleagues found that 81% (38/47) of countries in the WHO African Region included levodopa plus carbidopa or levodopa plus benserazide as a therapeutic alternative on national essential medicines lists, considering any formulation or strength. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-08-25) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12481222/
- [statement] Fothergill-Misbah and colleagues state that inclusion of Parkinson disease medicines in national essential medicines lists provides no guarantee of immediate access. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-08-25) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12481222/
- [statement] The BMJ modelling study projects 25.2 million people living with Parkinson disease worldwide in 2050, with a 95% uncertainty interval of 21.7 to 30.1 million. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-03-05) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40044233/

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/global-burden-economic-cost-and-access-to-pd-care/ · 16 claims from 11 sources

## Patient registries and research participation: PPMI and trial finders

Parkinson’s research participation spans observational biomarker cohorts, online studies, trial matching tools and genetic research. PPMI combines longitudinal biomarker research with online, mailed-screening and in-person participation routes. Fox Trial Finder connects volunteers with recruiting studies, while Fox Insight collects self-reported health experiences online. PDBP and the AMP Parkinson’s Disease platform support sharing of research data, and PD GENEration offers genetic testing and counseling. Participation opportunities coexist with incomplete demographic reporting and practical barriers documented in specific research populations. Foundation listings do not constitute endorsement of participation.

- [statement] The Parkinson’s Foundation says the Parkinson’s Outcomes Project, with 13,000+ participants, showed that the type and quality of care people receive has a major impact on their symptoms, mobility and long-term health. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinson.org/advancing-research/our-research/parkinsons-outcomes-project/findings
- [statement] The Parkinson’s Foundation states that the Parkinson’s Outcomes Project, started in 2009, was one of the largest-ever clinical studies of Parkinson’s disease, with more than 13,000 participants in five countries. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinson.org/advancing-research/our-research/parkinsons-outcomes-project
- [statement] The PPMI participant page states that academic and industry investigators can access the repository after administrative review and completion of a Data Use Agreement requiring privacy protection. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.ppmi-info.org/participants
- [statement] The Michael J. Fox Foundation describes Fox Trial Finder as a tool connecting volunteers with recruiting studies through searches based on location and health history, without requiring a login. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.michaeljfox.org/trial-finder
- [statement] The Parkinson’s Foundation describes PD GENEration as an international research study providing genetic testing and genetic counseling at no cost for people diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinson.org/advancing-research/our-research/pdgeneration

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/patient-registries-and-research-participation-ppmi-and-trial-finders/ · 16 claims from 14 sources

## Regulatory pathways (FDA, EMA) for PD therapies

Regulatory evidence for Parkinson’s therapies spans medicinal-product guidance, biomarker support and qualification, drug applications and approvals, and device supplements. EMA distinguishes its effective guideline from a concept paper proposing revision. Biomarker support letters have a narrower meaning than qualification. Concrete examples illustrate FDA drug applications, a device supplement, and distinct European authorisation routes. Sponsor announcements are attributed separately from regulator records. FDA’s discussion of real-world evidence also documents limits on its use in labeling.

- [statement] FDA’s novel-drug list records Juvmo, tavapadon, approved on 9/25/2026 for Parkinson’s disease in adults; AbbVie subsequently announced JUVMO approval on Sept. 28, 2026. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.fda.gov/drugs/novel-drug-approvals-fda/novel-drug-approvals-2026
- [statement] EMA’s DAT imaging letter supports further development and validation; the Stephenson review reports a subsequent full Qualification Opinion in 2018 for DAT enrichment in Parkinson’s trials targeting early motor symptoms. (low confidence) (verified as of 2019-07-30) — https://media.c-path.org/wp-content/uploads/20240427170245/cpp_ema_letter_of_support_cpp_imaging_biomarker-1.pdf
- [statement] FDA’s Onapgo approval letter identifies NDA 214056 as an application under section 505(b)(1) for apomorphine hydrochloride injection to treat motor fluctuations in adults with advanced Parkinson’s disease. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-02-03) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2025/214056Orig1s000ltr.pdf
- [statement] FDA’s safety summary identifies adaptive deep brain stimulation as device supplement P960009/S478 and dates its approval notice February 20, 2025; FDA’s roundup describes marketing approval on February 21. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-02-28) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cdrh_docs/pdf/P960009S478B.pdf
- [statement] FDA’s approval letter for NDA 216962 states that the application for Vyalev (foscarbidopa and foslevodopa) injection for subcutaneous use was submitted pursuant to section 505(b)(2) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. (low confidence) (verified as of 2024-10-16) — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/appletter/2024/216962Orig1s000ltr.pdf

Pack: https://llmsx.org/tree/regulatory-pathways-fda-ema-for-pd-therapies/ · 15 claims from 14 sources

# Contested findings, open questions and misbeliefs
Source: https://llmsx.org/tree/parkinson-s-disease/

## Contested

- Controversy: The Parkinson Foundation describes anticholinergics as predominantly useful for tremor with little effect on other symptoms; the Cochrane review found motor benefit over placebo but conflicting results and insufficient support for a preferential effect on tremor. The latter limits claims of established symptom selectivity. — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/treatment/prescription-medications/anticholinergic-drugs vs https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8728160/ · Amantadine, anticholinergics and other adjunct drugs
- Controversy: Naltrexone has not established overall efficacy for PD-related ICDs: the 2015 management review reports a negative primary global-response outcome but improved secondary QUIP-RS scores, whereas the 2024 review summarizes the trial as a failure to improve ICDs. Secondary scale improvement should not be represented as definitive treatment success.  ||  Naltrexone interpretation depends on the endpoint: the 2015 review describes a negative primary outcome with secondary QUIP-RS improvement, while the 2024 review summarizes failure to improve ICDs. These are different readings of the same trial, not independent efficacy replications. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5077247/ vs https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11098885/ · Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation
- Controversy: Evidence assessments differ for istradefylline: the MDS motor-fluctuation review rates it likely efficacious while noting inconsistent effects of unclear clinical relevance, whereas EMA’s Nouryant refusal assessment found efficacy insufficiently established. These attributed judgments should not be collapsed into a universal efficacy or availability claim.  ||  The MDS review rates istradefylline likely efficacious but notes inconsistent benefit of unclear clinical relevance; EMA’s Nouryant refusal assessment found efficacy not established. These are explicitly attributed judgments from distinct assessments. — https://movementdisorders.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mds.30162 vs https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/medicines/human/EPAR/nouryant · MAO-B, COMT inhibitors and adenosine A2A antagonists
- Controversy: Observational findings on medication delays and hospital length of stay conflict: Martinez-Ramirez and colleagues reported longer stays with delayed or missed doses, whereas Skelly and colleagues found no adjusted association; these findings do not establish that delays invariably prolong admission.  ||  The two observational cohorts report conflicting associations between medication delay or omission and length of stay; they differ in population and statistical adjustment. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4401689/ vs https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5292103/ · PD medication timing, interactions and hospital safety
- Controversy: The German consensus guideline allows methylphenidate to be considered for freezing, whereas the Espay trial authors report no gait benefit and a tendency toward worse outcomes; this is a difference between a permissive recommendation and a negative trial in a specific population.  ||  The German guideline permits consideration of methylphenidate for freezing; the Espay randomized trial reports no gait benefit and a tendency toward worse outcomes. These positions concern different levels of evidence and do not establish uniform benefit. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11561004/ vs https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3068005/ · Tremor, gait, freezing and postural instability management
- Controversy: The sponsor release says its results met both primary and secondary endpoints in the specified subgroups, while the paper states the study did not meet its primary endpoint of MDS-UPDRS Part II. — https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1477845/000110465924077093/tm2418712d1_ex99-1.htm vs https://www.nature.com/articles/s44400-026-00148-x · Alpha-synuclein aggregation inhibitors and buntanetap
- Controversy: Two sources give different sizes for the buntanetap subgroup with MMSE scores of 20 to 28: Alzforum reports 173 patients and the paper reports 182 participants. — https://www.alzforum.org/therapeutics/buntanetap vs https://www.nature.com/articles/s44400-026-00148-x · Alpha-synuclein aggregation inhibitors and buntanetap
- Controversy: FAIRPARK-II reported worse parkinsonism scores with deferiprone, whereas its trial team notes that 4 other trials in patients already on dopamine replacement drugs saw no worsening. — https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2209254 vs https://cureparkinsons.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/FAIRPARK-II-Statement-from-the-clinical-trial-team.pdf · Disease-modification trial landscape and lessons from failed trials
- Controversy: STEADY-PD III reported that isradipine did not slow clinical progression, while a re-analysis of STEADY-PD II data reports significantly smaller total and part 3 UPDRS scores with 10 mg/day ER isradipine than placebo at trial end, with post hoc adjustment for symptomatic therapy diminishing the statistical significance. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7465126/ vs https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8922308/ · Disease-modification trial landscape and lessons from failed trials
- Controversy: The ASPro-PD protocol gives the combined MDS-UPDRS parts I, II, and III score as the primary outcome, while the Cure Parkinson's page names the MDS-UPDRS Part III rating scale for motor symptoms. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12916515/ vs https://cureparkinsons.org.uk/research/research-projects/ambroxol/ · GBA1, ambroxol and lysosomal-targeted therapies

- Controversy: The specialist-team RCT and multidisciplinary-rehabilitation review report different quality-of-life results with different interventions and comparators; this limits blanket claims that every multidisciplinary model is superior. — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23165981/ vs https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8901313/ · Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- Controversy: Mirabegron bladder-trial findings differ: PaDoMi reported improved OAB symptom scores and another placebo-controlled PD trial reported positive primary outcomes, whereas MAESTRO found no significant primary composite-score benefit from adding mirabegron to behavioral modification. Results should be interpreted by population, comparator and endpoint. — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33389776/ vs https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34672847/ vs https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9682970/ · PD autonomic dysfunction: orthostatic hypotension, constipation, bladder
- Controversy: The 2019 MDS review called probiotics with prebiotic fiber efficacious and clinically useful on the basis of one trial; the 2022 meta-analysis instead concluded that evidence remained insufficient, noting few trials, heterogeneous preparations and high heterogeneity. These are attributed assessments with different evidence sets, not an unconditional endorsement of probiotics. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6916382/ vs https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9684193/ · PD autonomic dysfunction: orthostatic hypotension, constipation, bladder
- Controversy: Cognitive training has mixed evidence: the German guideline supports it for PD-MCI but notes small, heterogeneous trials; an eight-week computerized-training RCT in PD patients with subjective cognitive complaints found no benefit on primary planning accuracy and no group differences at follow-up. The populations and interventions differ, so this is a limitation on generalization rather than proof that every training program fails. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11561078/ vs https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35248830/ · PD cognitive impairment and dementia treatment
- Controversy: Galantamine recommendations also differ by guideline and date: the 2019 MDS review calls it possibly useful despite insufficient PD dementia efficacy evidence; the 2024 German guideline recommends against its use. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6916382/ vs https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11561078/ · PD cognitive impairment and dementia treatment
- Controversy: Memantine recommendations differ: NICE NG71 (2017) allows consideration only when cholinesterase inhibitors are contraindicated or not tolerated, whereas the 2024 German guideline recommends against memantine for PD dementia. — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations vs https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11561078/ · PD cognitive impairment and dementia treatment
- Controversy: Troche’s positive EMST swallowing-safety result coexists with Gandhi and Steele’s cautious systematic-review conclusion that lower-risk-of-bias studies supported efficiency rather than safety benefits; this is an evidence-certainty difference, not proof the trial result is false. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2995389/ vs https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9159671/ · PD dysphagia, sialorrhea, speech and voice problems
- Controversy: Experimental findings on sensory thresholds conflict: one study reported that thermal and mechanical pain thresholds were uninfluenced by levodopa or STN-DBS, whereas another reported significant increases in mechanical pain and tolerance thresholds after acute STN-DBS and after acute levodopa administration. A uniform direct effect on central pain processing is not established by these studies. — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20629160/ vs https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23864314/ · PD pain, fatigue and sensory symptoms
- Controversy: Conditional AASM support for immediate-release melatonin and a negative prolonged-release PD trial concern different formulations and do not establish a direct contradiction. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10071384/ vs https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31674060/ · PD sleep disorders: RBD, insomnia and daytime sleepiness
- Controversy: Brundin and Melki emphasize neuron-to-neuron propagation; Surmeier and colleagues challenge the explanatory sufficiency of the spreading hypothesis using human pathology and connectome evidence.  ||  Brundin and Melki propose neuron-to-neuron transfer as essential for regional Lewy pathology spread; Surmeier and colleagues argue that the spreading hypothesis is difficult to reconcile with human postmortem and connectome evidence. — https://www.jneurosci.org/content/37/41/9808 vs https://www.jneurosci.org/content/37/41/9799 · Alpha-synuclein biology and prion-like spread
- Controversy: Cui and colleagues contrast the classical opposing-pathways model with their mouse observation of increased activity in both pathways at action initiation. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4039389/ vs https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/jn.00527.2025 · Basal ganglia circuitry and dopamine neurobiology
- Controversy: Longitudinal prognostic results differ by analysis: a PPMI analysis found no statistically significant association between baseline seeding measures and progression among manifest patients, whereas a separate analysis associated baseline time-to-threshold with subsequent cognitive decline in PPMI and an independent Tübingen cohort. Diagnostic positivity should not be treated as an established general progression measure.  ||  One PPMI analysis reported no significant baseline SAA–progression association among manifest patients; a separate analysis reported cognitive-decline associations for time-to-threshold in PPMI and Tübingen cohorts. The analyses differ in method and outcome, so they are not replications of the same endpoint. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12354789/ vs https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40541208/ · Alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay and fluid biomarkers
- Controversy: FAME reported higher PD odds with paraquat use; the later prospective AHS analysis did not show a statistically clear association. Both draw on the Agricultural Health Study and are not independent cohorts.  ||  Tanner et al. reported an association between paraquat use and PD in FAME (110 cases, 358 controls; OR 2.5, 95% CI 1.4–4.7), whereas the later AHS prospective analysis reported no statistically clear association (HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.84–1.41). These overlapping study populations and different designs should not be counted as independent replications. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3114824/ vs https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7822498/ · Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution
- Controversy: Tanner et al. reported increased PD odds with paraquat; EPA states that it has not found a clear link for labeled uses. A paraquat systematic review and meta-analysis described a positive association without an indisputable causal conclusion.  ||  The paraquat evidence has conflicting interpretations: Tanner and colleagues’ 2011 Agricultural Health Study nested case-control analysis reported an association with PD (OR 2.5, 95% CI 1.4–4.7); EPA’s page updated November 3, 2026 states that it has not found a clear link between labeled paraquat uses and PD. The regulatory statement is qualified by labeled-use conditions. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3114824/ vs https://www.epa.gov/ingredients-used-pesticide-products/paraquat-dichloride vs https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31476981/ · Epidemiology and environmental risk factors: paraquat, TCE, air pollution

- Controversy: EANM/SNMMI regards persistent SWEDD as unlikely idiopathic PD; Palermo et al. describe selected older-onset clinical cases with initially normal imaging and argue for possible false negatives, while acknowledging absent pathological confirmation. This is a difference in scope and interpretation, not an established general false-negative rate. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7300075/ vs https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9092727/ · Imaging biomarkers: DaTscan, MRI and PET
- Controversy: One autopsy-based study supported Braak staging with an advanced-Alzheimer-pathology exception; Burke et al. questioned whether the observed anatomical patterns establish temporal progression. These are attributed interpretations with different emphasis, not proof that all patients follow a single sequence.  ||  Published interpretations differ: an autopsy-based study concluded that the PD staging scheme is valid except in the setting of advanced Alzheimer’s disease, whereas Burke and colleagues judged the evidence insufficient to establish the proposed caudal-to-rostral temporal progression of human Parkinson’s disease. — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20187227/ vs https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2605160/ · PD staging: Hoehn-Yahr, Braak and biological SynNeurGe

These are attributed interpretations, not proof of a universal sequence. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2605160/ vs https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neurology/articles/10.3389/fneur.2017.00037/full · PD staging: Hoehn-Yahr, Braak and biological SynNeurGe
- Controversy: The GUT-PARFECT paper title describes a phase 2 trial, whereas the registry record NCT03808389 lists phase NA, with the record status verified 2023-01. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11056595/ vs https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT03808389 · Gut-brain axis: microbiome and body-first versus brain-first PD
- Controversy: Two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled fecal microbiota transplantation trials in Parkinson's disease report different primary-outcome results, and they differ in delivery route, comparator and primary-outcome time point: the trial at 4 hospitals in Finland (FMT or placebo via colonoscopy; primary end point at 6 months) reports that the primary outcome did not differ between the groups, whereas GUT-PARFECT (nasojejunal FMT with healthy donor stool or the participant's own stool; primary outcome at 12 months) reports that the MDS-UPDRS motor score improved by a mean of 5.8 points in the healthy donor group and by 2.7 points in the placebo group (p = 0.0235). — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11287445/ vs https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11056595/ · Gut-brain axis: microbiome and body-first versus brain-first PD
- Controversy: Reports differ on motor progression in SAA-negative Parkinson's disease: an analysis of LRRK2 carriers reports less severe motor manifestations and decline without alpha-synuclein aggregates, while a European Academy of Neurology commentary on a PPMI analysis reports faster time to motor disability milestones in SAA-negative PD, with a relatively small sample. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11925012/ vs https://www.ean.org/research/resources/neurology-updates/detail/beyond-the-a-synuclein-seed-amplification-assay-shall-we-re-evaluate-the-biological-definition-of-parkinsons-disease · PD subtypes and precision medicine

- Open question: Amantadine is a weak uncompetitive NMDA-receptor antagonist; the Gocovri label states that its therapeutic mechanism is unknown and distinguishes anticholinergic-like adverse effects from demonstrated direct anticholinergic activity. — https://www.gocovrihcp.com/Gocovri_Digital_PI_MG.pdf · Amantadine, anticholinergics and other adjunct drugs

- Open question: Sources describe limited durability of cueing effects: the APTA guideline states that the lasting effects of cueing are unclear because benefits appear to dissipate over time, and that effects appear to dissipate when the cues are removed; the RESCUE crossover trial (153 patients; 3-week home cueing programme using a prototype cueing device) reported that effects of intervention had reduced considerably at 6-week follow-up; and a narrative review of cueing in people with freezing of gait reported that long-term consolidation and transfer of the effects appear to be hampered in that subgroup. — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2077658/ · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28890341/ · Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
